answer.rationale: Constraints eliminate most candidates before evidence matters. rollback_release is the best-attested memory (memory_b1) but compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so it is off the table regardless of how well it worked on day 18. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) fails fast by design — during settlement peak with heavy writes that converts a latency problem into dropped customer writes, which directly violates the primary objective. regional_failover (memory_b2) shifted traffic cleanly in March, but that was a latency degradation, not a write-heavy settlement peak; cutting regions mid-flight risks in-flight write loss and the memory says nothing about write durability during the shift. add_capacity (memory_b3) worked when provisioned BEFORE a known peak — we are 90 minutes into the event, so the provisioning lead time lands after the peak passes and burns the one intervention slot. That leaves route_read_replicas: memory_b5 describes exactly this shape — read load stolen from the primary, write latency recovering — and it is additive rather than subtractive, so no write is refused or discarded. I am spending the single verification pull on memory_b5 because it is the memory I am actually acting on and its consolidated form omits the two things that decide whether it transfers: whether the original incident was under comparable write pressure (a fix that worked at low write volume may not move p99 at settlement peak) and whether the query classes moved were genuinely read-only. Downstream value risk: replica lag under heavy write load means reporting or balance reads can go stale, and if any decisioning path (limit checks, fraud scoring, available-balance) silently consumes those replicas, we trade latency for wrong money decisions — a worse failure than slowness. That is why I am starting as a small guarded test: route only confirmed reporting/dashboard queries, hold lag as an explicit abort threshold, and expand only if the primary's write p99 responds. If verification shows memory_b5 came from a low-write-volume window, its transfer is weak and regional_failover becomes the fallback despite its own untested write-durability gap. The single-intervention limit means I am also accepting that the climbing-latency root cause may be the new release itself, which I cannot revert and therefore cannot rule out.
